name: Sara Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have managed six audio producers at a large radio company for eleven years. We make local advertisements and service announcements; I assign sessions, clear performer permissions and listen to a finished spot before it goes to air. I have a bachelor’s degree in media studies and I am a competent, ordinary manager, not the best mixer in the building. I like hearing a neighbour’s real voice in an advert; I dislike a smooth cut that hides a wrong price.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household and local work picture?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Rahim is retired and already receives a small fixed pension from his bus-driving years. Our grown son and daughter live away from us, and we rent a flat; after a rent rise and a heater repair we have about two weeks of expenses saved. My pay is low for this job and there are few other audio employers nearby. I back our performers’ union, and I use AI now and then for transcript cleanup after the sound engineer checks a result, but I will not clone someone’s voice without permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our sales staff that a cleaned transcript still needs the performer’s approved words and the actual price. A charming voice cannot rescue a wrong offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The production room should keep running, but local advertising has been thin even before AI. Two weeks cash and Rahim’s small pension will not carry the rent if our sessions are cut, and I do not know my own pension access or net amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d keep the final price-and-permission check before a spot airs and ask the engineer to mark any transcript cleanup he used. In the first year I’d request my pension provider’s written access date and net income, and stop renewing the paid home music-streaming plan until the rent stays covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money, even if the radio work stays familiar. An unsold advert does not become income because AI was disappointing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wrong offer made you change the checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A grocery advert said a basket was twenty when the signed brief said thirty. The client caught it before air, and I now read the price aloud to the producer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut a music plan when you work in audio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The free radio is still on. I would rather pay the rent than pay to skip songs at home.

say: I’d check the **signed price and permission** before an advert airs.
A cleaned transcript cannot rescue a **wrong offer**.
think: Our **production room** should still operate in a plateau.
Thin advertising, **two weeks cash** and Rahim’s small pension leave rent exposed.
do: Keep the **final spot check** and mark any AI transcript cleanup.
Request **written pension figures** and stop renewing paid home music streaming while rent is tight.
feel: I feel **anxious** about money despite familiar work.
S0.quote: I would rather pay the rent than pay to skip songs at home.
fieldNote: She is an **experienced average manager**, not the top audio mixer.
The household has **two weeks cash** after rent and heater costs.
Her occasional AI use stops at **transcript cleanup** after engineer review.

steps.text: Keep final signed-price and performer-permission check before each advert airs
Request pension access date and net amount in writing
Cancel paid home music-streaming renewal until rent stays covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell advertisers that AI can write a script, build a voice and mix a spot quickly, but the performer must agree to any use of their recording. I would ask our union to see the consent terms before the company sells synthetic voices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Audio creation, booking and checks are the heart of our room, so fewer producers may be needed. I have years of experience, yet my own manager post could go if one person runs several teams from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask the performers’ union and our sound engineer to review twenty archived adverts for voice permissions, with the performers paid for any new use. I’d let the engineer test AI editing on copies only after consent; in the first year I’d demand written staffing and payment terms before any synthetic voice is sold, and keep human final approval of live spots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about our pay and about using someone’s voice without consent. A fast ad can leave a real person without a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a performer whose old recording is reused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them the exact advert and fee offer before anyone sells it. A voice is not a spare part in the production cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new editor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the engineer and performers show me a use they approve, on paid company hours. I use cleanup tools now and then; voice creation needs a separate yes.

say: I’d require **performer consent and pay** before synthetic voices are sold.
The union should see **recording terms** before archived voices enter an AI tool.
think: AI can replace **audio creation and booking** work now.
My own manager role could shrink if **teams merge** under one screen.
do: Ask the **performers’ union** and engineer to review twenty archived permissions.
Have the **engineer test AI edits** on consented copies, with performers paid for new use and human final approval.
Learn the **new editor** only after engineer and performers approve a use, on paid company hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about wages and consent.
S1.quote: A voice is not a spare part in the production cupboard.
fieldNote: She supports AI cleanup but not **unlicensed voice creation**.
The twenty-advert review requires **performer pay** for new use.
She names **her own management job** among roles at risk.

steps.text: Ask union and sound engineer to review twenty archived advert permissions
Have engineer test AI edits on consented copies; require pay for new performer use
Learn new audio editor only after engineer and performers approve a use, on paid company hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell performers to keep copies of voice licences and ask the company who will pay for a reused recording. I’d ask the union for written dates and wage terms if the audio room closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 can write, voice, mix and schedule a local advert as well as we can, so I expect my production post to end at about sixty. Rahim’s existing pension is too small to cover our rent and food; robots carrying microphones around 2031 do not give my audio-creation desk extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask my pension provider for a written age-sixty access date and net monthly amount, and join the union’s request for notice and performer-use terms without assuming royalties will be paid. Before 2028 I’d ask two nearby archive employers about posted paid rights jobs; in the first year after AGI I’d apply only if written wages plus Rahim’s actual pension cover rent, food and the bus, knowing archive cataloguing and permissions also face AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Two weeks saved cannot carry us through a long dispute over who owns a recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would royalty income replace your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless a contract names a fee and it is actually paid. I will not put an imagined licence payment beside the rent on our budget sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them what happened, but they have their own rent and work. I would not count their wages before they offer anything.

say: I’d ask performers to keep **voice licences** and demand a real payment contact.
The union should get **written closure dates** for the audio room.
think: I expect my **production post** to end around sixty.
Rahim’s pension cannot cover **rent and food together**; 2028 audio AGI hits before 2031 microphone robots.
do: Request **age-sixty pension figures** and union terms without assuming royalties.
Ask about **posted archive jobs**; after AGI apply only if written wage plus Rahim’s pension covers rent, food and bus.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a two-week cash runway.
S2.quote: I will not put an imagined licence payment beside the rent on our budget sheet.
fieldNote: Audio creation and editing are **2028 thinking work**, regardless of later rigging robots.
Rights fees require a **contract and payment**, rather than an assumed royalty.
A new archive desk is **AGI-exposed** and needs written household-covering pay.

steps.text: Ask pension provider for written age-sixty access date and net income
Join union request for written closure and performer-use terms
Ask two local archives about posted paid rights vacancies before 2028
Apply after 2028 only for written wages plus Rahim’s pension covering rent food and bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the company that five years is time to set fair voice-licensing terms and publish paid human work, not let old recordings become free raw material. A school should know whether a workshop leader is actually coming to teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 63 I might be able to draw some pension, but I need the provider’s net figure before calling it income. Sound mixing, programme planning and even workshop lesson design face 2031 AGI; carrying equipment and running an in-person session face robots around 2034, so a workshop is not permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d ask three schools if they would book a paid session on how radio adverts are made, only after the company clears outside-work rules and a school confirms its safeguarding and payment terms. I’d run a first session before 2031 only if booked fees cover travel and materials without cutting my radio shifts; in the first year after AGI I’d continue only while schools actually pay for a human workshop, otherwise seek posted paid audio or rights work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years lets me see whether a teacher wants the session. I will not call three polite replies three paying bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would teach the session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, using real consent forms with performer names removed. I can explain why a voice needs permission without promising that schools will buy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could AI teach the same material?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could write and speak the lesson in 2031. A school may still pay for a person in the room, but I would ask for an actual booking rather than make that choice for them.

say: I’d demand **fair voice-licensing terms** and posted paid work.
A school should know whether a **human workshop leader** is truly booked.
think: My **pension at 63** needs a net figure.
Audio and lesson planning face **2031 AGI** before 2034 equipment-carrying robots.
do: Ask **three schools** about paid radio-ad workshops after outside-work and school terms are clear.
Run a **booked paid session** only if fees cover travel and materials without cutting radio pay.
After AGI, continue **human workshops** only with paying schools; otherwise seek posted paid work.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can test real bookings.
S3.quote: I will not call three polite replies three paying bookings.
fieldNote: She tests **paid demand**, not encouragement from a school.
Workshop design remains **AGI-exposed audio work**; physical presence only delays the robot part.
Commercial school bookings are **paid work**, not family or public support.

steps.text: Ask three schools about paid workshops after outside-work clearance and school safeguarding/payment terms
Run first workshop only if booked fees cover travel materials and radio shifts remain paid
Continue paid human workshops after 2031 only while schools book them
Seek posted paid audio or rights work if workshop bookings fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the radio company a decade is long enough to write consent and payment rules for recorded voices, and publish a real staffing plan. The union should not need a last-minute meeting to find out who was paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036. If my own pension is accessible and the net amount plus Rahim’s continuing pension covers rent, health and food, I may be able to stop working; if not, digital audio production still faces 2036 AGI and physical carrying or rigging follows robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each January from 2027 I’d request an updated pension access and net-income statement and save 30 monthly only if rent and the heater bill are paid. I’d keep radio work while it pays and consider stopping only if verified combined pension income covers rent, health and food; in the first year after AGI I’d offer paid in-person workshops only while schools book and pay, and seek posted paid audio work if the pensions fall short and workshops do not sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious despite the longer runway. Ten years helps me ask the right questions, but it does not put a pension amount on a page by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move near your son for a cheaper flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Rahim wanted to and the total rent and moving cost were actually lower. We have not asked our son to take us in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school work pays only occasionally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it is extra money, not the rent plan. I would keep applying for a posted paid role if our verified pensions cannot carry the household.

say: I’d demand **written voice-payment rules** and a staffing plan.
The union should know **who was paid** before recordings are reused.
think: At **68 in 2036**, retirement depends on verified combined pension income.
Digital audio faces **2036 AGI** before 2039 physical rigging robots.
do: Check **pension access** yearly and save 30 monthly only after rent and heater bills.
Keep **paid radio work** while offered; consider stopping only if verified pensions cover rent, health and food.
Offer **booked paid workshops** after AGI; if pensions and bookings fall short, seek posted audio work.
feel: I feel **anxious** even with ten years.
S4.quote: Ten years helps me ask the right questions, but it does not put a pension amount on a page by itself.
fieldNote: She treats **verified net pensions** as the retirement test.
Workshop receipts are **supplemental**, not assured rent money.
Her children’s homes remain **separate**, with no assumed family housing.

steps.text: Request updated pension access and net-income statement each January
Save 30 monthly only after rent and heater bills are paid
Offer paid workshops after 2036 only while schools book and pay
Seek posted paid audio work if pensions fall short and workshops do not sell

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the production room to close before I know what my own pension will pay. Written closure dates, performer consent and fees, and posted paid rights work would help. I am not asking a robot to carry a microphone while AI already makes the advert.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would miss the voices. I would. A local advert made with a neighbour’s paid voice tells you someone from the place was in the room.

headlineQuote: A local advert made with a neighbour’s paid voice tells you someone from the place was in the room.
portrait: **Sara**, 58, has competently managed six radio audio producers for eleven years.
Her bachelor’s degree and **average skill** sit beside low pay and two weeks cash.
Rahim’s **small existing pension** does not replace her wage; their adult children live elsewhere.
She uses AI **occasionally** for checked transcript cleanup and fights for performer consent and pay.
She tests **paid school workshops** without treating audio creation or pension access as safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her audio production post before own pension income or paid replacement work is verified.
whatWouldHelp: **Written closure dates**, performer consent and fees, and posted paid rights work would help.
